fact: English is the official international language of aviation and maritime communications worldwide.
The word 'Pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis' is the longest word in major English dictionaries, referring to a lung disease.
The pangram 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog' contains every letter of the English alphabet.
The word 'set' historically had more distinct dictionary definitions than almost any other word in English.
English is classified as a Germanic language, but over half of its modern vocabulary comes from Latin and French origins.
William Shakespeare added more than 1,700 words to the English language, including 'lonely', 'swagger', and 'uncomfortable'.
The letter 'E' is the most frequently used letter in written English, appearing in roughly 11% of all words.
The shortest complete sentence in English is 'I am.', consisting of a subject and a verb.
A 'ghost word' is a word that entered a dictionary purely by printer or editor error, such as 'dord' in 1934.
The dot over the lowercase letters 'i' and 'j' is called a 'tittle'.
There are no common English words that form a true rhyme with 'orange', 'purple', 'silver', or 'month'.
The word 'alphabet' comes directly from the first two letters of the Greek alphabet: alpha (Α) and beta (Β).
English used to have grammatical gender for nouns, just like modern German, French, and Spanish, until around the 13th century.
The word 'run' is projected to eclipse 'set' in future dictionaries as the word with the highest number of distinct meanings.
The ampersand symbol ('&') was once considered the 27th letter of the English alphabet in the 19th century.
A word created by combining two existing words, like 'brunch' (breakfast + lunch) or 'smog' (smoke + fog), is called a portmanteau.
Old English was written using a runic alphabet called Futhorc before adopting the Latin script.
The word 'clue' originally meant a ball of thread. Its modern meaning comes from the myth of Theseus navigating the labyrinth with thread.
More people speak English as a second or foreign language worldwide than native speakers of the language.
The term 'uncopyrightable' is one of the longest English words that can be spelled without repeating any letter.
English spelling became fixed largely due to William Caxton installing the first printing press in England in 1476.
The Great Vowel Shift between 1400 and 1700 fundamentally changed long vowel pronunciations in English, making spelling differ from pronunciation.
Words that are spelled the same backwards and forwards, like 'radar', 'level', and 'kayak', are known as palindromes.
The word 'sandwich' was named after John Montagu, the 4th Earl of Sandwich, who asked for meat served between two slices of bread.
English is one of the six official working languages of the United Nations, alongside French, Spanish, Russian, Chinese, and Arabic.
The expression 'O.K.' is one of the most recognized words on the planet, originating as a humorous misspelling of 'oll korrect' in 1839.
The word 'robot' entered English from a 1920 Czech play by Karel Čapek, derived from the Slavic word 'robota' meaning forced labor.
The sentence 'Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo' is a grammatically valid sentence in English.
The symbol '#' is officially called an octothorpe, though commonly known as the number, pound, or hashtag symbol.
English adopts new words constantly; dictionaries add over 1,000 new words or updated definitions every single year.
